stories.headline: Man shot during confrontation with campus police at Colorado State University in Fort Collins
stories.summary:
A man was injured Monday evening in a shooting involving police on the Colorado State University campus in Fort Collins. Campus police received a report around 5:35 p.m. of a man behaving erratically who approached a university officer with a handgun near Newton Plaza.

Gunfire occurred and the suspect was shot, according to campus officials. It was unclear whether the man shot himself or was struck by the officer's round. Aid was rendered and he was taken to a local hospital. No other injuries were reported.

The public was asked to avoid the area around the chemistry and microbiology buildings. The campus alert system showed an all-clear as of 6:50 p.m., though police remained in the area Monday night. The man's identity and condition had not been released. The Fort Collins Police Department is leading the investigation.

stories.headline: State report finds Aspen Acres Fire was sparked by aspen tree falling onto power line
stories.summary:
The Colorado Division of Fire Prevention and Control has published its initial report on the Aspen Acres Fire, one of the state's most destructive wildfires since the 2021 Marshall Fire. The Scripps News Group obtained the report Monday from attorneys representing fire victims.

Investigators concluded the fire began about 200 feet west of Colorado Highway 165 at mile marker 17, when high winds blew an aspen tree onto overhead power lines. The impact forced the lines to about three feet above the ground. The tree contacted both the hot and neutral conductors, and showed charring, while the lines showed arcing and melting. Melted aluminum found beneath the tree was cited as a possible contributor to ignition.

Investigators ruled out other causes. No lightning was recorded within five miles of the origin, no smoking materials were found, and no evidence pointed to an intentionally set fire. Burn patterns showed the fire spread west and south from the origin area.

stories.headline: Aurora leaders agree to meet with protesters demanding police chief's firing
stories.summary:
Two Aurora city councilmembers and the city manager agreed to meet Monday night with protesters demanding the firing of Police Chief Todd Chamberlain. The group, organized by Epitome of Black Excellence, said it would not leave the council building without a termination date and strategy.

City Manager Jason Batchelor, Public Safety Committee Chair Rob Andrews and Mayor Pro Tem Alison Coombs were to attend. Batchelor told The Denver Gazette the firing will not happen but that he is willing to listen. Chamberlain was chosen by Batchelor in August 2024, and critics say the process lacked community input.

Mayor Mike Coffman said Chamberlain has brought stability and that he should stay, citing a 38.8% drop in major crimes. Police data show about 16,300 reported crimes in 2024, 12,700 in 2025 and 8,500 so far this year, with eight homicides this year versus 30 last year. Protesters have attended council meetings for more than two years over police killings, including Kilyn Lewis in May 2024, Rajon Belt-Stubblefield in August 2025 and Amare Garlington in April 2026.

stories.headline: Denver Water pulls more from Western Slope to refill reservoirs, drawing Grand County pushback
stories.summary:
Denver Water is drawing more water from rivers, creeks and communities in Grand County to refill its reservoirs after a record-hot summer. The utility's reservoirs, which serve 1.5 million people, are far below normal for this time of year, and mandatory restrictions allow it to increase diversions from certain Western Slope streams.

Starting Tuesday, flow past a Fraser River gauge will drop to 2 cubic feet per second from about 4. Flows in late September over the past five years ranged between roughly 6 and 10 cfs. Vasquez Creek, the sole water supply for the town of Winter Park, will drop to 2 cfs from 3, and Ranch Creek fell to 1.5 cfs from 2 on Oct. 2.

Kirk Klancke of the Colorado River headwaters chapter of Trout Unlimited said Front Range residents did not conserve enough this summer. He warned that the Winter Park area's supplies will shrink and that fish eggs can die in shallow ice. The Fraser River is the sole water supply for Winter Park Ski Resort and feeds the Colorado River.

stories.headline: Denver City Council at-large vacancy candidates align on license plate cameras and zoning changes
stories.summary:
Nearly all candidates running to fill a vacant at-large seat on the Denver City Council say they will not support extending the city's contract for license plate-reading cameras. Most also want changes to the city's zoning overhaul proposal. The seat opened when Councilwoman Sarah Parady resigned in August, and it will be up for election again in April.

In a Denver Post questionnaire, most candidates said they would let the Axon contract expire in March unless the city first approves rules limiting law enforcement use of the data. Three said they would not approve the technology at all. Monica Martinez said she would renew only if analysis shows a meaningful public safety benefit.

Nine of the 10 candidates responded, with Julissa Soto not submitting answers. Most said they would support the updated Unlocking Housing Choices proposal with a few changes. The November election has no runoff and could be decided by a small number of votes.

stories.headline: Unpaid property taxes in Denver rise sharply as tax lien auction begins
stories.summary:
Denver begins its annual property tax lien auction this week, and the pool of delinquent taxes is growing. The cumulative value published by the city in September was $45.5 million, about 7% of the total. That is 25% higher than last year's $36.3 million and 74% higher than 2024's $26.2 million.

The number of six-figure delinquent parcels rose from 27 in 2024 to 35 in 2025 and 49 this year, likely reflecting distress in commercial real estate. Industrial properties were most represented with 13, followed by retail with nine. The largest bill belongs to the Denver Marriott Tech Center, owing $1.5 million, followed by the Pop Denver apartments, in foreclosure, at $965,000.

Not all will be auctioned. Last year only 56% of the published amount was ultimately sold, as many owners pay before auction. This year's auction runs from Oct. 12 to noon Nov. 4. Investors earn a 13% annual interest rate and may foreclose if a lien remains unpaid after three years.

stories.headline: CloudBees opens downtown Denver hiring hub; Texas de Brazil opens in Westminster
stories.summary:
Software firm CloudBees opened a downtown Denver hiring hub for engineering and product roles as it expands its presence in major global tech markets. The company's Boulder-based CEO led the opening of the hub.

Separately, Texas de Brazil opened at Orchard Town Center in Westminster. The restaurant represents a $5 million investment and is the chain's third location in the Colorado market.

Both openings point to continued business expansion in the Denver metro area.

stories.headline: Troy Guard's HashTAG opens in Wheat Ridge; Revel Strength & Wellness debuts in Central Park
stories.summary:
Chef Troy Guard's TAG Restaurant Group opens HashTAG Wheat Ridge on Thursday at The Lookout at Clear Creek Crossing, near Interstate 70 and Highway 58. The five-acre dining and entertainment district includes a public park with mountain views, an amphitheater, fire pits and a communal dining license. It is the group's first counter-to-table service model.

In Denver's Central Park neighborhood, Revel Strength & Wellness opened earlier this month at 2954 N. Havana St. The collective houses seven businesses, including a gym, yoga and Pilates studio, Apto Physical Therapy and Café Arrieros. The gym has about 250 members with capacity for about 600.

Also, law firm Akerman LLP named Erika Labelle managing partner of its Denver office, succeeding Kevin Hein. Labelle has almost 20 years of experience in transactional tax, REIT and controversy matters.

stories.headline: Colder weather and mountain snow suppress Colorado wildfire activity; Bear Creek Lake Park prescribed burn planned
stories.summary:
A strong cold front is moving across Colorado, bringing sharply colder temperatures, higher humidity and mountain snow that significantly suppress wildfire activity. Established fires in Custer, Lake and Douglas counties continue to hold within their perimeters, and recent small starts along the Front Range have been extinguished. No red flag warnings or fire weather watches are active.

West Metro Fire Rescue and the City of Lakewood planned a prescribed burn at Bear Creek Lake Park to clear grass fuels, with operations scheduled to begin around 10 a.m. Monday and potentially continue through the week as conditions permit. South Road access is closed, while campers retain access through the main entrance.

The Denver Gazette's weekly outlook calls for mostly sunny conditions Monday, rain and snow showers midweek, and gradual warming toward the weekend.

topStory.headline: Bipartisan Senators Demand Trump Reverse Russian Diesel Import Deal as Analysts Doubt Price Impact
topStory.summary:
President Donald Trump on Monday defended a plan to import diesel from Russia amid growing bipartisan calls in Congress to reverse it. "I made the right choice for the American People—always America first," Trump said. On Friday, he announced that after a discussion with Russian President Vladimir Putin, Moscow would "immediately" supply 300,000 metric tons of diesel to U.S. and global markets, followed by 500,000 tons in November and 1 million tons shortly after. According to Trump, Russia would then deliver another 3 million tons, depending on the condition of its refineries. The U.S. Treasury issued a temporary license easing sanctions on Russian diesel to facilitate the arrangement.

Seven senators released a joint statement Sunday saying the decision "runs directly counter" to a 2022 law banning Russian energy imports. The signers were Republicans Lisa Murkowski of Alaska, Susan Collins of Maine, Thom Tillis of North Carolina and John Curtis of Utah, and Democrats Jeanne Shaheen of New Hampshire, Ron Wyden of Oregon and Richard Blumenthal of Connecticut. They said the administration had not consulted Congress or explained its decision, and wrote: "The United States should not provide Putin with a financial lifeline while Russia continues to kill Ukrainian civilians. The Administration must immediately reverse course." Murkowski added that Congress recently passed legislation to increase sanctions and tariffs on Russia, and said Russia's return to global energy markets could be discussed once the war ends.

Other Republicans also voiced opposition. Sen. John Kennedy told The Washington Sun he does not support the move and called Putin a "butcher," while Rogers said he would not want to give Putin "an inch." A spokesperson for Sen. Dan Sullivan told The New York Times the senator believes American energy dominance, including more Alaska production, is the answer to high prices rather than imports from Russia. Rep. Don Bacon criticized Trump's approach to Russia in social media posts, saying the U.S. should not stand with the invader and pressure the victim to make concessions.

On Sunday, Trump also declared that Russia and Ukraine had agreed to an "energy ceasefire" effective immediately, a announcement that surprised policymakers, including in Kyiv. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said Monday that Russian strikes overnight and into the morning hit energy facilities and wounded 33 people, calling them violations of the ceasefire and "Putin's answer to Trump." He said Ukraine was awaiting details of U.S.-Russia conversations. Trump, responding over the weekend to Zelensky's initial criticism of the diesel deal, told reporters "it's time for Ukraine to get a new President." Oil prices fell Monday after the ceasefire announcement before rising later.

The deal comes as fuel costs have become a political liability for Republicans ahead of November's midterm elections, in which the party risks losing both chambers. Diesel prices reached a record average of $6.5276 per gallon in late September, according to AAA, and averaged $6.2665 on Monday, up from $3.6653a year earlier. Prices have climbed since the Iran war began in February, and farmers have told TIME that operations are severely affected. A Pew Research Center survey found 84% of registered voters consider the economy very important to their vote.

Analysts doubt the arrangement will significantly lower prices. Mohit Kumar of Jefferies said the agreed volumes are unlikely to make a substantial difference, and Lombard Odier analysts cautioned that announced shipments are not equivalent to delivered supply and that the deal does not restore damaged infrastructure or normalize maritime transport. Former International Energy Agency oil division head Neil Atkinson said the source of the volumes is "a mystery," noting that a recent G7-authorized release of 50 million barrels of oil products had made almost zero difference to diesel market tightness. Whether the administration revises the plan under congressional pressure, and whether the energy ceasefire holds, remain open questions.
